query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, structural and chemical stability over the catalytic/thermoelectric operating range (473–1923 K) is governed by a balance between high configurational entropy and lattice distortion. When the atomic size mismatch is small, the entropy-driven stabilization limits atomic diffusion and maintains a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution. Conversely, significant lattice distortion reduces diffusion barriers, allowing diffusion-driven segregation or short-range ordering to occur at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near‐equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA nanoparticles to controlled thermal treatments (e.g., thermal cycling or isothermal exposures) across the 473–1923 K temperature range under catalytic/thermoelectric relevant atmospheres.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under controlled inert or relevant reactive atmospheres with constant nanoparticle size, composition, and heating/cooling rates that mimic operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion arising from atomic size differences, which influences the rate and extent of atomic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, high configurational entropy tends to stabilize a disordered solid solution. However, if significant lattice distortion is present, the enhanced atomic diffusion can overcome the entropy stabilization, leading to phase segregation or the emergence of short-range chemical ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch (low lattice distortion) are expected to retain a uniform single-phase structure and stable catalytic/thermoelectric performance across the temperature range, whereas those with larger mismatches will show signs of phase change (e.g., secondary phases or compositional inhomogeneity) accompanied by performance degradation.
generation.baseline: The initial room-temperature state is a homogeneous, single-phase, random solid solution with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds under controlled testing conditions that replicate typical catalytic and thermoelectric operating environments; however, extremely long exposures or temperatures at the extreme upper limit may eventually challenge the stability even in entropically stabilized systems.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of lattice distortion at which phase segregation is triggered is uncertain and may vary with the specific combination of metals used.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with metals selected for minimal atomic size mismatch (low lattice distortion) and a control set with enhanced atomic size differences (high lattice distortion). Subject both sets to thermal cycling from 473 K to 1923 K under identical controlled atmospheres and processing conditions. Monitor structural evolution in real time via in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) and post-treatment characterization with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), alongside catalytic/thermoelectric performance measurements.
measurements: In situ XRD for phase identification and detection of any new phase formations
TEM/EDS for assessing elemental distribution and detecting signs of short-range ordering or segregation
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance metrics during and after thermal treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the minimal and the higher lattice distortion nanoparticle sets maintain an indistinguishable, homogeneous single-phase structure and exhibit comparable performance over the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion (mediating atomic diffusion) governs the loss of stability is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are solid solutions consisting of five or more metallic elements in approximately equimolar ratios with elemental compositions typically between 5–35 atomic percent (at.%). They have attracted increasing attention, especially as structural materials, due to their remarkable mechanical strength and resistance to oxidation and fatigue at ambient and elevated temperatures. The compositional complexity does not automatically imply microstructural complexity due to the high mixing entropy. Often, an operational definition for HEAs is a solid-solution phase stabilized by the higher configurational entropy that increases with increasing temperature. With increasing the number of alloying elements (N), it should be noted, however, that the entropy increases as N ln N whereas interacting pairs that may drive chemical order increase as N2; so at low temperatures any favorable ordering enthalpy could overcome the slower increasing entropy – a point often not given its due importance. It should be noted that our atomistic modeling results are consistent with the prediction based on simple thermodynamic calculations, confirming the tendency of the given quinary composition to form a single solid-solution phase. More importantly, the structural similarity at the different temperatures (from 573 to 1000 K) underlines the high thermal stability of the HEA nanoparticles, consistent with the observation from the catalytic durability studies (see Table 2).

In contrast to conventional alloy materials based on single principal elements, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have recently received considerable attention in various fields because of their unique physical and chemical properties. In principle, HEAs are produced by alloying five or more metal elements in nearly equal proportions (recently extended to 5 to 35 at%) into solid solutions with a high mixing entropy rather than an intermetallic phase. The resulting synergistic effect endows HEAs with high mechanical strength, good thermal stability, and catalytic activity. In particularly, HEAs displayed appraisable catalytic performance in electrocatalytic water splitting, ammonia oxidation and decomposition, and CO2 reduction. Mechanistic studies suggest that the ligand effect and distortion effect of HEAs, which arise from tuning the composition and geometric properties of HEAs to a large degree, could significantly modify the electronic properties of active sites and consequently improve their catalytic performance. The inherent synergy effect of HEAs provides possibility to boost the catalytic activity by combining suitable metals.

drafts.hypothesis: In equal-atomic‐ratio, five-metal nanoparticles initially crystallized as a single solid solution, high configurational entropy stabilizes the lattice against phase segregation at elevated temperatures—but only when the constituent metals have minimal atomic size mismatch. With larger atomic size differences, the increased lattice strain accelerates local diffusion and surface segregation, leading to loss of structural and chemical homogeneity under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K).
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios forming a single-phase solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Subjecting differently composed nanoparticle batches, chosen to vary mainly in their degree of atomic size mismatch, to high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions (473–1923 K).
drafts.conditions: Operating under controlled atmospheres (avoiding extraneous reactions) and keeping all synthesis and processing variables constant except for atomic size mismatch, across the specified temperature range.
drafts.structural_mediator: The interplay between high configurational entropy and lattice distortion (due to atomic size differences) that affects local metal diffusion kinetics and the tendency for surface segregation.
drafts.mechanism: At lower atomic size mismatches, high configurational entropy overcomes the modest kinetic driving force for diffusion, preserving a homogeneous solid solution. However, when atomic size differences are significant, lattice distortions enhance diffusion and promote phase segregation, undermining the initial uniform structure.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch will maintain a stable single-phase solid solution with consistent catalytic and thermoelectric performance over the 473–1923 K range, whereas those engineered with larger atomic mismatches will display phase segregation (detected as secondary phases or heterogeneous elemental distributions) and concomitant performance changes.
drafts.baseline: The initial state is a homogeneous, single-phase nanoparticle with equal or near-equal elemental distribution and stable catalytic/thermoelectric properties at room temperature.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies under controlled-synthesis and high-temperature test conditions; extreme temperatures near the upper limit (close to 1923 K) may challenge even the best-entropically stabilized systems, and uncontrolled atmospheres could introduce additional variables.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one with minimal atomic size mismatch and one with intentionally larger atomic size differences (achieved by selecting metals with more disparate atomic radii) but otherwise identical synthesis conditions. Expose both sets to a controlled high-temperature environment (473–1923 K) under catalysis/thermoelectric operating conditions. Monitor the phase evolution in real time using in situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) and assess elemental distribution through transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS).
measurements: Phase composition and evolution via in situ XRD
Catalytic and thermoelectric performance metrics over temperature cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with minimal atomic size mismatch show similar levels of phase segregation or performance degradation as those with larger mismatches under the same temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that high configurational entropy stabilizes the single-phase structure under these conditions would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles, the ability to maintain a structurally and chemically stable single-phase solid solution across 473–1923 K is governed by the balance between high configurational entropy and the diffusion‐driven tendency for elemental segregation, which is amplified by intrinsic differences (e.g., atomic size, chemical potential) among the constituent metals.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios, crystallized as a single-phase solid solution at room temperature.
drafts.intervention: Thermal treatment spanning catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions (473–1923 K) with variation in elemental mismatch (e.g., comparing sets with minimal vs. enhanced differences in atomic radii or chemical potentials).
drafts.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert atmospheres with identical synthesis, particle size distribution, and surface characteristics; absence of reactive ambient species that might independently drive chemical changes.
drafts.structural_mediator: The onset of elemental diffusion leading to detectable phase segregation (such as second-phase precipitates or compositional gradients) acts as the mediator between the intrinsic thermodynamic driving forces and the observable loss of stability.
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, increased atom mobility enables diffusion processes that tend to separate elements according to their individual chemical potentials and sizes. When these diffusive forces exceed the stabilizing contribution of high configurational entropy, phase segregation occurs, compromising the chemical and structural integrity of the nanoparticle; the threshold for this transition is determined by the magnitude of the mismatch between the metals.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered with metals that have minimal differences in atomic size and chemical potential should retain their single-phase solid solution structure over the full thermal range, whereas those with enhanced mismatch should display evidence of phase segregation (e.g., formation of secondary phases or compositional inhomogeneity) when subjected to high-temperature conditions.
drafts.baseline: The initial as-synthesized nanoparticles exhibit a single-phase, chemically homogeneous solid solution at room temperature.
drafts.boundary: This prediction applies under inert environmental conditions and when particle size, synthesis method, and surface characteristics are controlled. In reactive or oxidizing environments, additional processes could obscure the role of intrinsic elemental mismatches.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic five-metal nanoparticles: one set using metals with closely matched atomic radii and similar chemical potentials (low mismatch) and another set where one or more elements are chosen to introduce significant atomic size/chemical potential differences (high mismatch). Subject both sets to controlled thermal cycling from 473 K to 1923 K in an inert atmosphere. Monitor the phase stability during heating using in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (XRD) and post-process with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) coupled to energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to assess compositional uniformity.
measurements: In-situ high-temperature XRD to detect phase changes or new phase emergence
TEM imaging to evaluate microstructural integrity
EDS mapping to analyze elemental distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the low-mismatch nanoparticles exhibit comparable phase segregation or compositional inhomogeneity (i.e., detection of secondary phases or significant elemental clustering) under the high-temperature regime as observed in the high-mismatch group, then the hypothesized balance between configurational entropy and diffusion-driven segregation is disproven.

drafts.hypothesis: The retention of the single-phase solid solution state in equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles over the catalytic and thermoelectric operating range (473–1923 K) is governed by the balance between high configurational entropy and lattice distortion. When the intrinsic atomic size differences are kept minimal, the high entropy stabilizes the random solid solution even at elevated temperatures; however, if the lattice distortion (i.e., atomic size mismatch) exceeds a critical threshold, it triggers unfavorable short-range ordering and phase separation that undermines both structural and chemical stability.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios forming a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Systematic variation of the constituent metal mix to introduce different levels of lattice distortion (i.e. minimal versus increased atomic size mismatches) while maintaining overall equiatomic ratios.
drafts.conditions: Thermal and operational cycling under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions within 473–1923 K in an inert or controlled reactive atmosphere.
drafts.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion (atomic size mismatch) which mediates short-range ordering versus sustained solid-solution behavior.
drafts.mechanism: A competition between the entropy-driven stabilization of a disordered solid solution and the enthalpic driving force for atomic ordering or segregation induced by lattice strain. Minimal atomic size mismatches favor a high entropy state that resists phase separation, whereas excessive lattice distortion increases local energetic inhomogeneities that promote segregation or intermetallic formation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with minimal lattice distortion will retain their homogeneous, single-phase structure and exhibit stable catalytic and thermoelectric performance across the entire temperature range, whereas those with higher lattice distortion will show signs of phase separation or increased short-range ordering, leading to degraded performance.
drafts.baseline: High-entropy nanoparticles initially synthesized as uniform solid solutions with minimal atomic size differences among constituent metals.
drafts.boundary: The prediction holds provided that other factors (such as oxidation or extrinsic impurities) are controlled, and that the atomic size difference remains below a threshold similar to the conventional ~15% limit set by Hume–Rothery rules.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles: one set using metals with very similar atomic radii (low lattice distortion) and another set intentionally incorporating a metal with a significantly larger atomic radius (high lattice distortion). Subject both sets to thermal cycling within 473–1923 K under inert atmosphere, and periodically characterize their crystal structure and catalytic/thermoelectric performance.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and detection of any phase separation or ordering
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for nanoscale structural examination
Catalytic turnover frequency and/or thermoelectric performance metrics measured at various stages of the thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-lattice-distortion nanoparticles maintain a single-phase solid solution structure and exhibit performance metrics statistically indistinguishable from the low-distortion control samples over the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs the loss of stability is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: The ability of HEA nanoparticles to maintain a single-phase solid-solution structure over the catalytic/thermoelectric operating range (473–1923 K) is governed by a balance between high configurational entropy and the kinetic hindrance provided by lattice distortion. When the entropy term is large enough and lattice distortion is sufficient to slow atomic diffusion, even modest attractive interactions between specific elemental pairs cannot overcome the entropy-driven mixing, preserving stability. Conversely, if the attractive mixing enthalpy between certain elements becomes dominant relative to the entropy gain and if lattice distortion is insufficient to limit diffusion, short-range ordering or phase separation will emerge.
drafts.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in near-equiatomic ratios, crystallized as a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with random atomic arrangement.
drafts.intervention: Subject the HEA nanoparticles to controlled thermal cycling (or isothermal treatments) across the 473–1923 K range under catalytic/thermoelectric relevant atmospheres.
drafts.conditions: Experiments performed under inert or catalytic/thermoelectric operating atmospheres with constant nanoparticle size and composition; controlled heating/cooling rates that simulate operational environments; parallel samples with varying degrees of atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy to serve as controls.
drafts.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion (due to atomic size differences) and the extent of short-range chemical ordering, which govern the atomic diffusion rates.
drafts.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, high configurational entropy favors a random solid solution by lowering the free energy despite favorable enthalpic drives for ordering. Simultaneously, severe lattice distortion increases diffusion energy barriers, retarding atomic rearrangements that would otherwise lead to phase separation. If in a given composition the attractive enthalpic interactions overcome these stabilizing effects, local ordering or decomposition will occur, degrading the catalytic/thermoelectric function.
drafts.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles engineered with moderate atomic size differences (ensuring sufficient lattice distortion) will maintain a single-phase structure and uniform catalytic/thermoelectric performance across the 473–1923 K range, whereas compositions with higher attractive chemical interactions and lower distortion will exhibit phase changes (e.g., detectable secondary phases or increased chemical ordering) upon thermal cycling.
drafts.baseline: The initial room-temperature state where the nanoparticles present a homogeneous, random single-phase solid solution.
drafts.boundary: This prediction holds for operational timescales relevant to catalytic/thermoelectric applications. Over extremely long high-temperature exposures beyond typical operational conditions, even entropy-stabilized systems might slowly evolve.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with optimized elemental selections to maximize lattice distortion and minimize atomic size mismatch (and thus strong enthalpic attractions), and a control set with a higher propensity for attractive interactions (through larger atomic size differences or known ordering pairs). Subject both sets to thermal cycling from 473 K to 1923 K under identical catalytic/thermoelectric atmospheres. Use in situ structural probes (X-ray diffraction, TEM, and XPS) combined with performance measurements (catalytic activity or thermoelectric output) throughout cycling.
measurements: Phase composition and crystallography (via in situ XRD and TEM)
Catalytic or thermoelectric performance metrics over temperature cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both HEA sets show similar retention of a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with no detectable signs of phase separation or short-range ordering—and with constant catalytic/thermoelectric performance—despite differences in lattice distortion/atomic size mismatch, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion and enthalpic balancing govern the stability is falsified.
